name: The Pratfall Effect
statement: A small blunder makes a highly competent person more likable, but makes an average one less so.
statementAccent: makes a highly competent person more likable, but makes an average one less so
meaning: The pratfall effect is the tendency for a blunder or minor mistake, a pratfall, to change a person's likability in a way that depends on their perceived competence. When a highly competent, near-flawless person commits a small blunder, they tend to become more likable, appearing more human and approachable; when an average or mediocre person commits the same blunder, they tend to become less likable. The effect was demonstrated in a 1966 study by Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman, and Joanne Floyd, in which listeners heard a recording of someone answering quiz questions and then, in some versions, clumsily spilling a cup of coffee. A highly competent contestant who spilled the coffee was rated the most likable of all, while an average contestant who spilled it was rated the least likable. The effect shows that a well-placed imperfection can enhance the appeal of the highly capable while worsening that of the ordinary.
mechanism: The explanation centres on relatability and social distance. A person who appears extremely competent, even near-perfect, can seem intimidating or hard to identify with, creating psychological distance; a minor, harmless blunder humanises them, showing they are fallible like everyone else, which reduces that distance and increases warmth and liking. For an already average or mediocre person, there is no intimidating perfection to soften, so the same blunder simply adds another negative note, confirming or worsening the modest impression and lowering likability. The effect thus hinges on the interaction between competence and the mistake: the blunder helps only when it offsets an image of daunting excellence. It concerns minor, relatable mishaps rather than serious failures, and research has found that its strength can be moderated by characteristics of the observer, including self-esteem and gender, so the effect is not uniform across all people.

examples.text: In the 1966 study, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled coffee was rated most likable, while an average contestant who spilled it was rated least likable.
A near-flawless expert who makes a small, harmless slip seems more human and approachable, narrowing the distance that intimidating perfection creates.
Marketing that admits a small weakness can build trust and relatability, an application of the idea that minor imperfections can increase appeal.

variants.name: The competence interaction
variants.text: The core feature that a blunder raises likability only for the highly competent, while lowering it for the average, so the effect depends on prior competence.

variants.name: Observer moderators
variants.text: The finding that the strength of the effect can vary with the observer's own characteristics, such as self-esteem and gender.

whyItMatters: The pratfall effect is a classic finding in the social psychology of interpersonal attraction, showing that likability is shaped not only by competence but by the interaction between competence and small human failings. It refines the intuition that we simply prefer the most capable people, revealing instead that a touch of fallibility can make the highly competent more appealing while doing the opposite for the ordinary. The effect has practical resonance in leadership, public speaking, branding, and personal relationships, where admitting a minor weakness can build trust and warmth for those already seen as skilled. As a memorable demonstration that perfection can be off-putting and that relatability matters, it remains a widely cited example of how impressions of people are formed, and of why a well-placed imperfection can be an asset rather than a liability.

working.text: note that the effect depends on how competent the person is first perceived to be, since the blunder's impact hinges on that.
add a small, harmless mistake, which humanises a near-flawless person but merely adds a negative to an average one.
expect the highly competent to become more likable and the average to become less, with observer traits moderating the size.

limits: The pratfall effect concerns minor, relatable blunders, not serious failures, and its direction depends on the person's perceived competence, so it is not a general rule that mistakes endear. Its strength is moderated by features of the observer, including self-esteem and gender, so it does not hold uniformly, and some specific claims about these moderators come from follow-up studies whose exact findings should be treated with care. The original demonstration used a particular audio-recording setup, and real-world applications, such as brands admitting flaws, are illustrative extensions rather than controlled tests. So while the core interaction between competence and blunder is a well-established classic, the effect's magnitude and boundaries vary with the mistake, the person, and the audience.
misreadings: The effect is not that mistakes make anyone more likable; a blunder helps only the highly competent and actually hurts the average, so the interaction with competence is essential. It applies to minor, harmless slips, not to serious errors, which do not humanise but damage. And it is not uniform across observers, since self-esteem and gender can moderate it, so treating the pratfall effect as a reliable trick for anyone to seem more likable by fumbling misreads a finding that depends on already appearing highly capable.
origin: Demonstrated by Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman, and Joanne Floyd in their 1966 study The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness, using a quiz recording in which a contestant spills coffee.
